name: Sitting-rising test
summary: Sit down on the floor and stand up again using as little support as you can. It scores, from 0 to 10, the strength, flexibility, balance and coordination needed for an everyday movement.
howTo: Use a flat, non-slippery floor with about 2 x 2 metres of clear space. Be barefoot.
Start standing. Without worrying about speed, sit down on the floor and then stand up again, using the least support you think you need.
Sitting down and standing up are scored separately, each out of 5 points. Total = 0 to 10.
Subtract 1 point each time you use a hand, a forearm, a knee, the side of a leg (the sides of the feet don't count), or a hand on a knee.
Subtract 0.5 points each time you partly lose your balance or the movement is unsteady.
You may try a few times after a demonstration or advice; keep the best sitting score and the best rising score.
A second person scoring from the side, or a video, makes the score more reliable than judging yourself.
safety: Have someone nearby, and clear the area of furniture and sharp edges.

Don't do it if you can't safely get down to and up from the floor, have had a recent hip, knee or back operation or injury, or have been told you have a high risk of falling. Ask your doctor or physiotherapist first.
Stop if you feel pain, dizziness or chest pain.
If you have osteoporosis, joint replacements or a balance problem, check with your doctor before trying it without support.

norms.label: Brazil (Brito 2014, 51–80)

source.title: Ability to sit and rise from the floor as a predictor of all-cause mortality

norms.population: 2002 adults aged 51–80 (68% men) tested at a clinic in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; median follow-up 6.3 years, 159 deaths.
norms.note: The study's four score groups, not age norms. Compared with 8 to 10, death rates were higher in the lower groups: hazard ratios 1.84 (6 to 7.5), 3.44 (3.5 to 5.5) and 5.44 (0 to 3), adjusted for age, sex and BMI. Each extra point went with 21% better survival. Age- and sex-specific scores exist (Araújo 2020) but were only available as an image, so they are not used.

evidence.claim: Among adults aged 51-80 tested at a clinic in Brazil, those with lower sitting-rising scores were more likely to die over about 6 years. Each extra point was linked to about 21% better survival.
whyThisGrade: Observational (retrospective cohort): shows a link, not that improving the score lengthens life.
One clinic's patients (68% men), not a random sample of the population.
Adjusted only for age, sex and body mass index; other health problems could explain part of the link.
159 deaths; the lowest-score group (0-3) had about 5 times the risk of the highest (8-10) (HR 5.44, 95% CI 3.1-9.5).

studies.title: Ability to sit and rise from the floor as a predictor of all-cause mortality

evidence.claim: In a larger group from the same research team (4282 adults aged 46-75, followed for a median of 12 years), people with the lowest scores (0-4) had about 4 times the risk of a natural death and 6 times the risk of a heart or blood vessel death compared with people who scored 10.
whyThisGrade: Observational cohort; a link, not cause and effect.
Same research group and study design as the 2014 study (participants probably overlap), so not an independent confirmation.
68% men; clinic patients rather than a population sample.
Adjusted for age, sex, BMI and clinical variables; the interval for heart and blood vessel deaths is very wide (HR 6.05, 95% CI 2.29-20.94).

studies.title: Sitting-rising test scores predict natural and cardiovascular causes of deaths in middle-aged and older men and women

evidence.claim: In US adults (Project Baseline Health Study), lower sitting-rising scores went together with being female, less education, fatty liver disease and high blood pressure, among other factors; people 65 and over averaged 5.4 points against 7.7 for younger adults.
whyThisGrade: Cross-sectional: measured at one time, so it can't show what comes first.
Exploratory statistical screening of many variables; the authors say the findings need validating.
Funded by a company (Verily Life Sciences).

studies.title: Factors associated with lower quarter performance-based balance and strength tests: a cross-sectional analysis from the project baseline health study

limits: It mixes several abilities (strength, flexibility, balance, body size) into one number, so it can't tell you which one is limiting.
Scoring is a judgement (what counts as unsteady); self-scoring is less reliable than a trained tester.
Practice improves the score; a higher score after practice does not necessarily mean better health.
The mortality studies come from one clinic in Brazil and one research group; they show a link, not that training the movement makes people live longer.
The age and sex reference values in this file were read from a secondary image, not from the original paper.
Pain, joint replacements or injuries can lower the score for reasons unrelated to general fitness.
A low score is not a diagnosis.
